background.definition: HAV infections cause acute, self-limited necroinflammatory disease of the liver that does not result in chronic infection or chronic liver disease. Hepatitis A is diagnosed by both a clinical picture of viral hepatitis and a positive HAV-IgM, which can last for up to 6 months.

list.listitem: The incidence of hepatitis A decreased to 4/100,000 population in 2014 with an estimated 2,500 cases after adjusting for under-ascertainment and under-reporting. The number of reported cases to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), however, increased from 1,390 cases in 2015 to 2,007 cases in 2016 resulting in an estimated number of new HAV cases in 2016 of 4000. This was largely due to two outbreaks linked to imported foods.

Outbreaks as of July 2021 were ongoing in 27 states according to data from the CDC, with case totals over 2 to 4 years ranging from 5132 in Kentucky to 34 cases in Vermont. Hospitalization rate was 61% overall.
Based on U.S. news reports from 1993-2011, 192 HAV-infected food handlers were reported and 34 (18%) transmitted HAV to restaurant patrons.
The U.S. incidence rate decreased since the implementation of routine vaccination in children until 2014, as noted above. Infection rates are highest in the elderly (>74 years).
The estimated U.S. annual direct and indirect costs were from $300 million to $488.8 million in 1997.

The average cost per hepatitis A–related hospitalization in the United States in 2017 was $16,232 (95% CI $15,052–$17,411). Average costs ranged from $12,921 in the West North Central Census Division to $19,680 in the Pacific Census Division.
One-third to two-thirds of the patients with hepatitis A are hospitalized.
Among 27 food-related outbreaks related to produce recorded in Canada between 2001 and 2009, only two were attributed to hepatitis A.
Hepatitis A infection is caused by HAV.
The infection is transmitted via the fecal-oral route by person to person contact or via contaminated food or water.
The number of reported cases of HAV and norovirus due to contaminated fresh produce has increased in several countries. The most frequent type of produce involved was frozen raspberries.
Hepatitis A is a 27 nm RNA picornavirus. The incubation period is 28 days (range: 15-50 days).

HAV replicates in the liver, is excreted in the bile, and is then spread in high concentration in feces from 2 weeks prior to 1 week after onset of symptoms. Children can shed virus for up to 10 weeks following infection.
Viremia occurs early in infection and can persist several weeks after symptom onset; blood-borne transmission of HAV is uncommon.
Pathologic changes in the liver are due to host immune response; antigen-specific T lymphocytes are responsible for destruction of hepatocytes.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Travelers to developing countries (especially Mexico, Central/South America and Africa)
Persons with sexual or household contact with a person with hepatitis A
Men who have sex with men
Users of injection and non-injection drugs
Persons working with HAV-infected nonhuman primates or with HAV in the research laboratory
Persons with chronic liver disease - no increased risk of infection but increased risk of fulminant hepatitis A

list.listitem:
Hepatitis A vaccination is recommended as 2 doses at least 6 months apart for all children age 12 to 23 months A and for those with risk factors (see Table 1). B
The CDC notes that one dose of single-antigen hepatitis A vaccine has been shown to control outbreaks of hepatitis A.
All persons who have been in close personal contact with a patient with HAV and who have not been previously vaccinated should receive immune globulin. C
Postexposure immunization for hepatitis A is recommended. B
After exposure to HAV, screening of contacts for immunity is not recommended, as it would delay postexposure immunization.

The U.S. as well as other high-income regions (e.g., Western Europe, Australia, New Zealand, Canada) have very low HAV endemicity levels and a high proportion of susceptible adults. Authors of a systematic review of studies conducted in the European Union or European Economic Area found that 24 countries had a very low HAV seroprevalence profile compared with five countries in 1975-89.
Screening of internationally-adopted children may be warranted. In one study, 30 of 656 children screened (4.6%) were acutely HAV infected.
Hepatitis A vaccination is recommended routinely for all children age 12 to 23 months. Other indications are shown in Table 1.

Vaccination status is strongly associated with acute liver failure (ALF) from HAV. Authors of a scoping review found a point prevalence of HAV-induced ALF in countries with no routine HAV immunization of 2% to 81% (combined rate of 27%; 95% CI 13%-43%), while the prevalence in countries with routine HAV immunization at the time of data collection ranged from 1% to 2% (combined of rate of 2%; 95% CI 1%-3%).

An intervention including on-site screening, motivational-enhanced education and counseling, on-site vaccination, and case management was successful in improving HAV vaccination rates among patients on methadone maintenance.
Vaccination of high-risk groups lags behind recommendations, with one study showing that only 43% of childcare workers were vaccinated against hepatitis A.
There are three licensed vaccines. Two are single-antigen vaccines and one (TWINRIX) is a combination vaccine for HAV and hepatitis B. All are inactivated vaccines.

Current dosing and schedules can be found on the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention website. VAQTA is given in a dose of 25 U to children and 50 U in adults. HAVRIX is given in a dose of 720 enzyme linked U to children and 1440 ELU to adults. TWINRIX is only licensed for adults, in a dose of 720 ELU or 20 mcg.
All vaccines are given in a series of two immunizations, the first no earlier than 12 months of age and the second 6 to 18 months later.

Co-administration with measles, mumps, rubella, varicella vaccines appears safe and effective, although seroresponse for varicella-zoster virus was not fully demonstrated. Co-administration of human papilloma virus (HPV-16/18) vaccine and hepatitis A and B vaccine also appears immunogenic and well tolerated.

Hepatitis A vaccine confers 95% protection for up to 10 to 25 years.
Authors of two Cochrane reviews concluded that pre-exposure prophylaxis vs. no vaccination significantly reduced the number of children and adult patients with hepatitis A at 6 to 12 months (RR 0.45 and 0.53, respectively and 0.09 for individuals not previously exposed to hepatitis A).

Although both an inactive and live attenuated HAV vaccines have been tested and found to be effective against clinically apparent hepatitis A, only the inactive vaccine has adequate data for assessing adverse effects which were comparable to placebo.
Observational study data support the safety of hepatitis A and hepatitis B vaccine administration during pregnancy.

Based on data from 5 clinical trials conducted in the US in children aged 12 to 23-months found protective antibody concentrations in 100% of toddlers after two doses and 92% after a single dose of inactive HAV vaccine. Adverse events (AE) were reported in 69.4% when HAV vaccine was administered alone and 71.1% when given concomitantly with other pediatric vaccines. The most common solicited injection-site AEs were pain/tenderness in about one quarter and redness in 13.6% (first vaccination) and 15.1% (second vaccination). The most common vaccine-related systemic AEs were fever (≥100.4ºF, 12.2%) and irritability (8.1%). Serious AEs were rare at 0.4% and only 0.1% were considered vaccine related.

The series confers immunity for at least 10 years in healthy adults, and no booster is recommended. Based on a recent paper, there is long-term persistence of hepatitis A vaccine-induced antibodies, with estimates of seropositivity rates ≥95% for at least 25 years. Even with single dose inactivated hepatitis A vaccine, protective anti-hepatitis A virus antibody levels persist for over 10 years; antibody levels increase or reappear after booster vaccination. Protection from HAV can be assumed for 4 weeks after having received the first dose.

Single-dose vaccination resulted in a high HAV seropositive rate and seroprevalence for at least 5 years among Chinese children. However, among patients who were using immunosuppressive medication, single-dose vaccination resulted in only 60% having a protective antibody level. Seroprotection rates reached 95% after the second dose.

Among HIV-infected men having sex with men, serologic response to three and two doses of HAV vaccine appears similar, although in a 5-year follow-up study, those receiving the 3-dose vaccine had greater sustained seroprotection (79% vs. 76% for intention-to-treat and 94% vs. 88% in the per-protocol analysis).

The most recent ACIP recommendations (2020) are to give HAV vaccine to all healthy persons not previously fully vaccinated (2 doses) who are aged ≥12 months and exposed to hepatitis A in the past 2 weeks. In addition, immune globulin may be administered to persons aged >40 years depending on the provider's risk assessment due to lower immunogenicity of vaccination in older individuals. TWINTRIX is not recommended for post-exposure prophylaxis.

Postexposure HAV vaccine and immune globulin (single IM dose, 0.1 mL/kg) should be given in different anatomic sites as soon as possible after exposure to all persons who are immunocompromised or have chronic liver disease and have not previously received HAV vaccine series. Vaccination with immune globulin protects against HAV for 3 months.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 6 trials of post-exposure prophylaxis found use of immunoglobulin more effective than no intervention or inactive control (RR of hepatitis A in adult patients 0.53; 95% CI 0.4-0.7); one trial showed immunoglobulin to be more effective than placebo. There was no significant difference between immunoglobulins and inactivated hepatitis A vaccine in seroconversion to hepatitis A vaccine antibodies at four weeks but the vaccine was more effective at 8 to 24 weeks.
Hepatitis A infection most commonly presents with jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, abdominal pain, fatigue, fever, nausea, and vomiting with elevated AST/ALT and bilirubin. B
Positive anti-HAV IgM, in the clinical setting of acute hepatitis, is required for the diagnosis of HAV infection. C

list.listitem: Diagnosis of hepatitis A requires both a typical clinical presentation of acute hepatitis and detection in the serum of anti-HAV IgM.
Most common presenting symptoms are jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, fatigue, fever, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and headache.
The severity of HAV infections can range from asymptomatic or very mild to fulminant hepatitis.

The severity of the symptoms is age dependent; over 80% of patients have jaundice except for those less than 5 years and over 60 years, where jaundice occurs in under 60%. The disease is asymptomatic in 70% of children under 6 years of age.
The most common findings on physical exam are jaundice (70%) and hepatomegaly (80%).

Acute pancreatitis associated with non-fulminant acute HAV is rare at 0 to 0.1%. Most reported cases occurred in Asian patients with a median interval between onset of jaundice and pancreatic pain of 4 days (range: 0-30) and 9% of cases in this systematic review were severe.

Anti-HAV IgM antibody is required for diagnosis. Anti-HAV IgM is detectable 5 to 10 days before onset of symptoms and remains positive for more than 6 months. IgG anti-HAV appears 14 to 21 days into the infection and provides lifelong immunity.
An alternative test with slightly lower but still acceptable accuracy is rapid dot immunogold filtration assay. Another such test with low but acceptable accuracy is ELISA of urine specimens.

In a case series of 136 hospitalized patients with acute severe hepatitis, a qualitative HAV RNA polymerase chain reaction test had equivalent diagnostic accuracy for hepatitis A compared to IgM anti-HAV. The test appeared to be more sensitive during the window period when IgM is negative or equivocal.
Typical laboratory findings include markedly elevated AST and ALT (>1000 U/L, usually ALT>AST), elevated alkaline phosphatase, and elevated direct and total bilirubin (5-40 mg/dL).
Also check hepatitis B and C serology, both to rule out acute infection and to diagnose, as HAV infection has a worse clinical course in individuals with underlying liver disease.

For patients with severe clinical manifestations, check CBC, PT, PTT, albumin, electrolytes, and glucose. In one case series of 47 inpatients with hepatitis A, a creatinine value >2 mg/dL was the best predictor of fulminant hepatitis and death.
The identification of hepatitis virus-specific induction of host proteins may be useful in differentiating the cause of infection and in studying viral clearance.
Patients with acute infection typically present with dark urine, fatigue, jaundice, fever, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, abdominal pain, and headache.
Check AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, and hepatitis A, B, and C serology.

Once the diagnosis of acute HAV is made by a positive anti-HAV IgM, evaluate for extrahepatic manifestations, including acalculous cholecystitis, pancreatitis, hematologic disorders, neurologic disorders, renal disorders, vasculitis, and arthritis.
The treatment of acute hepatitis A infection consists of rest and rehydration; hospitalization is required in up to 60% of patients. B
Patients with severe symptoms such as vomiting, dehydration, and signs of hepatic decompensation should be admitted. B
In the case of fulminant liver failure, liver transplant may be required. C
No drugs are indicated for HAV.
Liver transplant should be considered for fulminant liver failure.
Most patients require supportive care only: rest, oral fluids, and no hepatotoxins (alcohol, acetaminophen).
Reasons to hospitalize patients with hepatitis A are based on clinical grounds: dehydration, coagulopathy, encephalopathy, or hepatic decompensation.
Supportive care with hydration.
Hepatitis A is an acute necroinflammatory disease of the liver with a mortality rate of <2% and no long-term sequelae. B
Overall case fatality ratio is 0.3% to 0.6%, and up to 1.8% in those age 50 years or older. B
The four phases are incubation, prodromal, icteric, and convalescent. The patient is infectious 2 weeks before and 1 week after jaundice occurs. C
Incubation phase: lasts 10 to 50 days; the patient is asymptomatic but still transmits the disease.
Prodromal phase: lasts 3 to 9 days; initial symptoms are anorexia, fatigue, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, fever, diarrhea, dark urine, pale stools.

Icteric phase: begins within 10 days of initial symptoms, can last 8 weeks; as jaundice develops, fever generally improves. Viremia ends, although feces remain infectious for 1 to 2 weeks. Occasionally liver necrosis occurs, resulting in high fever, abdominal pain, vomiting, jaundice, and hepatic encephalopathy.

Convalescent phase: slow resolution of disease, with no lasting sequelae. Relapsing hepatitis occurs in 3% to 20% of patients in 4 to 15 weeks after initial symptoms. Persistent or chronic HAV infection has not been observed.
The case-fatality rate is 0.3% to 0.6%.
The case-fatality rate is up to 1.8% in age >50 years.
Authors of a scoping review of homeless populations found 10 outbreaks of HAV infection reported, with lethality rates ranging from 0 to 4.8%.
In fulminant hepatitis the mortality rate is 70% to 90%.

Despite the decrease in reported cases through 2014, HAV-related hospitalizations increased from 7.3% in 1999 to 24.5% in 2011. The mean age of hospitalized cases increased from 36.0 years in 1999 to 45.1 years in 2011; death rates, however, declined and mean age at death among decedents with HAV infection increased from 48.0 years in 1999 to 76.2 years in 2011.
Follow ALT/AST every 1 to 2 weeks until levels normalize (4-12 weeks).
High serum alpha-fetoprotein level is an independent predictor for early recovery.
Patients with HAV should avoid food handling and unprotected sex until they are noninfectious (2 weeks before, 2 weeks after jaundice).

The predominant risk factors from 2005 to 2007 data were international travel (45.8%), contact with a case (14.8%), employee or child in a daycare center (7.6%), exposure during a food or waterborne common-source outbreak (7.2%), illicit drug use (4.3%), and men who had sex with men (3.9%); vaccination should be considered for these risk groups and for those with chronic liver disease.
Patients >50 years have a worse clinical picture, require more frequent hospitalization, and have a higher mortality rate from fulminant hepatitis.
Hepatitis A vaccine appears safe to give during pregnancy, and should be given if there is a medical indication. Hepatitis A immune globulin is not contraindicated during pregnancy or lactation.
Acute HAV infection in the second and third trimester is associated with high risk of maternal complications and preterm labor.
Children are often asymptomatic or have a milder clinical course.
Routine vaccination is recommended for all children age 12 to 23 months, and this has decreased the incidence of HAV in the general population.

feature.caption: Hepatitis A Guideline Recommendations.
feature.feature_body:
Organization Recommendation
Center for Disease Control and Prevention Offer to these high-risk groups: People who use drugs (injection or non-injection) People aged ≥1 year experiencing unstable housing or homelessness Men who have sex with men People who are currently or were recently incarcerated People with chronic liver disease, including cirrhosis, hepatitis B, or hepatitis C Unvaccinated travelers to countries with high or intermediate hepatitis A endemicity*
Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, 2020
All children 12-23 months All children and adolescents aged 2-18 years who have not previously received HepA vaccine All persons aged ≥1 year infected with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) Adults at risk of hepatitis A (as above) or at risk of severe disease from hepatitis A Pregnant women who are at risk for HAV infection during pregnancy (e.g., international travelers, persons who use illegal drugs, persons who have occupational risk for infection, persons who anticipate close personal contact with an international adoptee, or persons experiencing homelessness) or for having a severe outcome from HAV infection (e.g., persons with chronic liver disease or HIV) During hepatitis A outbreaks, vaccinate persons aged ≥1 year who are at risk for HAV infection (see CDC above) Those providing services to adults in which a high proportion of persons have risk factors for HAV infection (e.g., health care settings for those who use illegal drugs, group homes, and nonresidential day care facilities for developmentally disabled persons)
American Academy of Pediatrics (2011)
Household members and close contacts, including baby-sitters, when children are adopted from countries with high or intermediate rates of hepatitis A infection, ideally 2 or more weeks before the child arrives
European League Against Rheumatism
Individuals with autoimmune inflammatory rheumatic diseases at risk, along with hepatitis B and herpes zoster vaccination, during quiescent disease, preferably prior to the initiation of immunosuppression
*https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/69/rr/rr6905a1.htm#F3_down Information from: https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/69/rr/rr6905a1.htm, PMID 30763295, 21949136, and 31413005
